title: Solar Orbiter traced a magnetic switchback back to the Sun
freshness: Peer-reviewed Nature Astronomy paper and ESA release published on October 8, 2026, within the preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: Solar Orbiter flew through a large kink in the solar wind's magnetic field and measured the particles inside it. Their chemical fingerprint traced the structure to hot magnetic loops near the Sun, showing how reconnection can launch a switchback before waves and turbulence reshape it in space.
whyItMatters: Magnetic switchbacks are common close to the Sun, but their origin has remained disputed. Linking one directly to a process in the solar corona helps explain how plasma escapes into the solar wind and offers a better physical basis for models of the Sun's influence throughout the Solar System.
whatToExploreNext: Can the same particle-fingerprinting method show whether smaller switchbacks share this origin or form later through turbulence?

sources.label: Coburn et al. in Nature Astronomy

body:
## A kink with a chemical address

Solar Orbiter flew through an S-shaped fold in the solar wind's magnetic field and found particles that carried an address from the Sun. The mixture of charged oxygen and carbon inside the fold matched plasma from hot, closed magnetic loops in the solar corona. By combining that chemical fingerprint with images and magnetic-field models, researchers traced the structure back to a process called interchange reconnection.

The solar wind is a continuous outflow of charged particles, or plasma, threaded by the Sun's magnetic field. Close to the Sun, spacecraft often encounter switchbacks: sudden bends in which the magnetic field turns sharply and can briefly point back toward the Sun. They are not simple changes in the field's overall polarity. A useful picture is a flexible hose with a travelling kink, though the real structure is a wave in plasma and magnetic field rather than a solid tube.

Scientists have debated two broad explanations. Switchbacks might be released by magnetic activity in the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere. Alternatively, waves and turbulence in the solar wind might generate them after the plasma has already escaped. Earlier observations linked switchbacks to regions near the solar surface and even imaged an S-shaped structure, but the precise formation process remained uncertain.

## What Solar Orbiter measured

The new study examined one unusually large switchback that Solar Orbiter crossed while it was roughly halfway between Earth and the Sun. The spacecraft's Solar Wind Analyser measured ions inside the structure. Different temperatures and magnetic environments in the corona leave different charge states and elemental proportions in escaping plasma, so this composition acts like a record of where the material formed.

The oxygen and carbon signature pointed to plasma that had been confined in hot coronal loops. Those loops are closed magnetic structures: their field lines rise from the Sun and return to it. Nearby open field lines instead extend outward and give plasma a route into the solar wind. Interchange reconnection occurs when closed and open fields meet and rearrange. A formerly closed loop can open, releasing trapped plasma and launching a magnetic disturbance along the outward field.

The team then connected the in-place particle measurements with Solar Orbiter images, observations from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, and a model of the magnetic field between the Sun and the spacecraft. The combined evidence led them to infer that interchange reconnection released this switchback. Signs of wave activity and turbulence were also present, suggesting those processes altered the structure as it travelled outward. The two competing ideas may therefore describe different stages of the same event.

## One event, a broader test

What was measured is the composition and magnetic structure of one exceptionally large switchback, together with a modeled connection to its solar source. The conclusion that interchange reconnection launched it is an inference supported by those linked observations. It does not prove that every switchback begins this way. Smaller structures or switchbacks in other streams may have different histories.

That limitation also points to the next test. If future crossings show the same hot-loop fingerprint, researchers can learn how common this route is. A clearer account of how plasma leaves the corona can improve models of solar-wind heating and acceleration. It also helps connect processes near the Sun with the changing magnetic conditions that spacecraft and planets encounter farther out.
